why: With at most 20 organisms there is no trick: the task is to implement the round rules exactly. A list of (family, size) plus a per-round 'already took part' flag, scanned left to right with deletions applied immediately, reproduces every example. This is the week's linked-list + simulation pairing; a Python list with deletions is the linked list here.
hints: Model one round precisely: who may act, in which order, and what 'participated' means after a deletion shifts the line.

Scan left to right. An organism that has not participated tries its left neighbour first (different family, strictly smaller, neighbour not participated), then its right neighbour. The eater is marked; the eaten one is deleted on the spot, so the next comparison sees the new neighbour.
Repeat rounds until a round has no meal, then return the largest survivor as 'family size'. Each round is O(n^2) at worst with list deletions, and there are at most n - 1 meals: trivial for n <= 20.
pitfalls: Equal sizes never eat each other (strictly smaller only), and same-family neighbours never eat each other.
An organism that ate this round cannot be eaten later in the same round, nor eat again.
Left neighbour has priority over the right one.
When the eater consumes its left neighbour, its own index shifts down by one; keep the scan pointer and flags aligned.
